endorse

/en-DORS/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Endorse means to publicly declare your support or approval for a person, plan, or product — to officially put your name behind it.

The teachers' union voted to endorse the candidate who promised smaller class sizes, and nine out of ten dentists endorse the toothpaste in the striped tube.

Example

After reading the safety report, the city council agreed to endorse the new bike-lane plan at a public meeting.

The council isn't just privately liking the plan — they are publicly and officially declaring their support for it, which is exactly what endorse means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

back: To back something is to support it — with money, votes, or public words — and the word is broad and informal. To endorse is narrower and more formal: you publicly attach your name and approval to it, the way an athlete endorses a shoe brand.

advocate: To advocate is to argue actively for a cause — making the case, urging others, pressing the reasons. To endorse can be a single formal act: you declare your support and lend your name, even if you never argue a word of the case yourself.

promote: To promote something is to push it into public attention — advertising it, talking it up, boosting its sales or turnout. To endorse is to state your own approval of it; a company can promote a product its executives never personally endorse.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

oppose: to stand against

reject: to refuse to accept

Where it sits · how publicly and actively you back it — approve → endorse → champion

approve vs. endorse: To approve a plan is simply to accept it — you can approve something quietly, with a nod or a signature, and never mention it in public, while to endorse it means publicly putting your name behind it.

champion vs. endorse: To champion a plan goes beyond endorsing it: a champion doesn't just declare support once, but actively fights for the plan at every opportunity.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-

Prefix — en-: to put on or in (from Latin in-)

Root — dorse

Root — dorse: the back (from Latin dorsum) — people signed the back of a document to show support

Put it together

Put it together: Endorse literally meant to write on the back (dorsum) of a document — signing the back of a check or contract to show your official approval. From that physical signature, it grew into any public declaration of support.

Use the root in a new word: dorsal

Use the root in a new word: dorsal: The shark's dorsal fin — the fin on its back — sliced silently through the calm water.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Public / formal

Endorse shows up in politics (a mayor endorses a candidate), in advertising (an athlete endorses a shoe brand), and in banking (you endorse a check by signing its back). The related noun form, endorsement, names the public declaration of support itself.
